proposal.utterance: A contract is a legal document.

entities.label: Contract
entities.rationale: A contract is an information artifact whose content (the agreement terms, obligations, rights) can be encoded in multiple physical media (paper, digital file, oral record). It is paradigmatically a generically dependent continuant — it can be copied, its content is what matters, and it depends generically on some bearer but not on any one specific bearer. This parallels the existing Statute class.

entities.label: LegalDocument
entities.rationale: A legal document is an information artifact — a generically dependent continuant — whose content carries legal significance (statutes, contracts, deeds, judgments, etc.). It serves as the superclass under which both Contract and the existing Statute class can be subsumed.

relations.rationale: LegalDocument is a kind of generically dependent continuant: it is an information artifact whose content can be instantiated in multiple physical copies.
A contract is a kind of legal document — the utterance asserts exactly this subsumption.
Statute (already in the ontology as BFO_0000031) is also a kind of legal document; connecting it here is conservative reuse that maintains consistency and takes advantage of the new superclass.

open_questions: Should 'LegalDocument' also be connected to or distinguished from 'LegalForm' (already in the ontology as BFO_0000031)? LegalForm appears to cover the formal/structural aspect of law rather than document artifacts per se, but clarification would help avoid overlap.

Is 'Contract' intended here as a class of all contracts (e.g., sales contracts, employment contracts) or as a specific kind such as a written contract? This affects whether further subclasses are needed.

Should a Contract bear instances of LegalObligation and LegalRight (already in the ontology), expressed via a has-part or some other relation between the generically dependent content of the contract and those role/obligation individuals?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance 'a contract is a legal document' introduces two ontological commitments: (1) there is a kind called Contract, and (2) there is a kind called LegalDocument, with Contract subsumed under LegalDocument. Both are best typed as generically dependent continuants (BFO_0000031) because they are information artifacts — their identity is constituted by their content rather than any particular physical instantiation, and that content can be copied across media. The existing Statute class is already typed as BFO_0000031 and is naturally a sibling of Contract under the new LegalDocument superclass, so I also assert that subClassOf relation as a conservative and consistency-preserving step. No individuals are introduced because the utterance expresses a general kind-level claim.

proposal.utterance: The parties to a contract are persons.

entities.label: ContractParty
entities.rationale: Being a party to a contract is an externally grounded social role inhering in a person. It is context-dependent (requires a contract) and is not an intrinsic disposition, hence Role rather than Disposition.

entities.label: Contract
entities.rationale: A contract is an information artifact whose content (obligations, rights, terms) can be instantiated in multiple copies or media. It is a generically dependent continuant — the canonical BFO typing for legal and documentary information objects.

entities.label: Person
entities.rationale: A person is a material entity with mass and spatial extent. This is the standard BFO typing for human beings. Roles such as ContractParty inhere in persons.

relations.rationale: ContractParty is a subclass of Role (BFO_0000023), capturing that it is an externally grounded realizable inhering in a bearer.

An OWL restriction encoding that every ContractParty inheres in (RO_0000052) some Person. This encodes the assertion 'parties to a contract are persons'. NOTE: this relation requires a named restriction class; the reasoner should interpret it as: ContractParty subClassOf (RO_0000052 only Person).

open_questions: Should 'Person' here mean only natural persons (human beings), or also legal persons (corporations, states)? If both, we may need a superclass 'LegalPerson' or a separate 'NaturalPerson' / 'JuristicPerson' distinction.

Should 'Contract' be typed as BFO_0000031 (generically dependent continuant, i.e. information content) or should we also distinguish the physical document (BFO_0000040) from the contractual content? Typically the content is GDC and the paper copy is a material entity.
Do you want to assert that every ContractParty role is realized in some process of contract formation or contract execution (BFO_0000054 realized in)?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance 'the parties to a contract are persons' introduces three ontological commitments: (1) there exist things called contracts, best typed as generically dependent continuants (BFO_0000031) because their content is the legally significant entity and can be copied across media; (2) there is a role class ContractParty (BFO_0000023) that inheres in bearers; and (3) the bearers of the ContractParty role are Persons (BFO_0000040, material entities). The relation between ContractParty and Person is modeled via BFO's inheres-in (RO_0000052), expressed as an OWL subClassOf restriction so that every instance of ContractParty must inhere in some Person. No existing working-ontology individuals or classes cover these concepts, so three new classes are minted. Key open questions concern whether 'person' includes juristic persons and whether we want to reify contract formation as a process.

payload.utterance: A contract realizes a disposition in each party, namely the capacity to contract.

proposal.utterance: Offer and acceptance are phases of contract formation.

entities.label: ContractFormation
entities.rationale: Contract formation is a happening that unfolds in time — a process in which parties move from negotiation to binding agreement. Typing it as Process (BFO_0000015) is well-grounded.

entities.label: Offer
entities.rationale: An offer is a communicative act that unfolds in time — a process. It is a temporal phase of contract formation, hence a process that is part of a ContractFormation process.

entities.label: Acceptance
entities.rationale: An acceptance is likewise a communicative act unfolding in time — a process. It is a temporal phase of contract formation, hence a process that is part of a ContractFormation process.

relations.rationale: ContractFormation is a subclass of Process (BFO_0000015).
Offer is a subclass of Process (BFO_0000015).
Acceptance is a subclass of Process (BFO_0000015).
Every Offer is part of some ContractFormation, expressing that Offer is a phase (temporal part) of ContractFormation. BFO_0000050 (part of) is the appropriate parthood relation between processes.
Every Acceptance is part of some ContractFormation, expressing that Acceptance is a phase (temporal part) of ContractFormation.

open_questions: Should 'ContractFormation' be restricted to bilateral contracts, or should it cover unilateral contracts as well (where acceptance may be by performance rather than a communicative act)?
Are there additional phases of contract formation to be added (e.g., Consideration, Capacity, Legality of object) that should also be modeled as sub-processes?
Should 'Offer' and 'Acceptance' be further typed as communicative acts (e.g., subclasses of a SpeechAct or CommunicativeAct class), or is plain Process sufficient for now?
Is the ontology intended to represent offer and acceptance as process types only, or should specific named instances (e.g., a particular contract's offer) also be added?
proposal.rationale_summary: The utterance asserts that Offer and Acceptance are phases — i.e., temporal parts — of ContractFormation. In BFO 2020, all three are best typed as Process (BFO_0000015) because they are occurrents that unfold in time. The mereological claim 'Offer and Acceptance are phases of ContractFormation' is rendered using BFO's part-of relation (BFO_0000050) expressed as OWL subclass axioms of the form 'Offer subClassOf (part_of some ContractFormation)', which HermiT can validate. No existing working-ontology classes cover these concepts, so three new classes are minted. The relations capture both the BFO type hierarchy and the process-parthood structure asserted by the utterance.
